## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: How to Read Your Monthly Marketing Report, Which Numbers Matter and Which Are Decoration

The numbers that matter in a monthly report from a digital marketing agency in Pune are the ones that sit close to money: enquiries and orders attributed to each channel, what each of those cost you, and how many of the enquiries turned into real sales conversations. Impressions, reach, likes, followers and "engagement" can be useful context, but they are not results, and a report that leads with them while hiding enquiries and cost is telling you something. This guide shows how to read a report line by line, what to ask when a number looks too good, and how to build a one-page version you can check each month.

It is written for business owners and marketing heads at Pune clinics, schools, builders, manufacturers, retailers and NGOs who receive a PDF each month, nod politely, and do not know whether to be pleased. We do not quote benchmark conversion rates or "good" cost-per-lead figures, because they vary enormously by industry, ticket size and city, and we cannot source a universal number. Where a benchmark would help we tell you how to build your own.

### Start with the question the report must answer

Every report should answer one question: did the marketing spend produce business, and was it worth it? Everything else is supporting evidence. So read the report in this order.

1. **How much was spent, in total, including the agency fee and the ad spend?**
2. **How many enquiries or orders did that produce?**
3. **How many of those enquiries were genuine?**
4. **How many became sales, or at least qualified conversations?**
5. **What did each genuine enquiry and each sale cost?**
6. **What changed since last month, and why?**

If the report cannot answer the first five questions, ask for a version that can. The sixth is where a good agency earns its fee, by explaining causes and proposing actions.

### The hierarchy of metrics

It helps to sort every number into one of four levels. Closer to the top is closer to revenue.

| Level | Examples | How much weight it deserves |
|---|---|---|
| Business outcomes | Sales, revenue, booked appointments, admissions, donations | The final judge. Often lives in your own records, not the agency's dashboard |
| Lead outcomes | Enquiries, calls, form submissions, WhatsApp chats started, qualified leads | The main thing the agency can directly influence |
| Behaviour | Website visits, clicks, time on page, pages per visit, video views | Useful for diagnosing, not for judging |
| Visibility | Impressions, reach, followers, likes | Context only; easy to inflate and weakly tied to results |

An agency that reports mostly at the bottom two levels is describing activity. One that reports at the top two is describing results. Neither is dishonest by default, but you should know which one you are reading.

### Reading paid advertising numbers

If the agency runs Google Ads or Meta ads, the report should include at least these lines, per campaign rather than only as a total.

**Spend.** Check it against the invoice from the platform or your payment card statement. Spend should match. Our guide to [onboarding access and tracking](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-onboarding-access-tracking-checklist-2026/) explains why the ad account should be in your name so you can verify this yourself.

**Clicks and click-through rate.** These show whether the ad is attractive. A low click-through rate usually means weak ads or the wrong audience. They do not show whether the clicks were valuable.

**Cost per click.** A diagnostic number. A rising cost per click with falling enquiries is a warning. A low cost per click with no enquiries is also a warning, since cheap clicks from the wrong people are worthless.

**Conversions, and what counts as one.** This is the most important line and the most misleading. A "conversion" is whatever the account has been told to count. It might be a purchase, a form submission, a phone call, or something trivial like a page scroll or a click on the WhatsApp button. Ask: which actions are counted as conversions in this account, and why? If the answer includes weak actions, the conversion count will look healthy while real enquiries are poor.

**Cost per conversion.** Divide spend by conversions, and then do the same sum yourself with genuine enquiries only. The gap between the two is the gap between the platform's view and your reality.

**Search terms and placements.** For search campaigns, the report should show the actual searches that triggered ads. Our guide to [search terms and negative keywords](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-terms-negative-keywords-2026/) shows what to look for. For Meta, check which placements and audiences produced results.

### Reading SEO numbers

SEO reports often lean on rankings screenshots. Rankings are a diagnostic, not an outcome, so look further.

**Organic clicks and impressions from Search Console.** These come directly from Google. They show how often your site appeared and how often people clicked. Ask the agency to show them for the pages they worked on, and compare the same period last year if you have the data. Google's [Performance report help](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) explains what the report shows.

**Queries, split into brand and non-brand.** Searches that include your business name are people who already know you. Growth in non-brand queries, such as the service plus the area, is the evidence that SEO is reaching new people. A report that celebrates total clicks without separating the two can be flattering you with your own brand traffic.

**Enquiries from organic search.** Visits are not enquiries. The report should show form submissions, calls and chats that arrived from organic search, using analytics set up to record them.

**Rankings, with context.** A keyword at position three means little if nobody searches for it. Ask for the search volume or, better, the impressions Search Console records for that query.

**What was actually done.** SEO is slow, so the report should list the work completed: pages written or improved, technical fixes made, links earned and listings updated. If a month's report says "ongoing optimisation" with nothing specific, ask what was changed.

### Reading social media numbers

Social reports are the most prone to decoration. Followers and likes feel good and cost little to inflate.

**Reach and impressions** tell you how widely posts were shown, but not whether the right people saw them.

**Engagement rate** can be defined in several ways, so ask how it is calculated.

**Follower growth** matters only if the followers are customers or likely customers. A rise of several hundred followers from outside your service area is not an enquiry.

**Actions that matter:** profile visits that led to website visits, direct messages asking about services, WhatsApp clicks and enquiries that can be traced to a post or campaign.

For organisations where social media supports reputation more than sales, that is a legitimate goal, but the report should say so and measure what it can: saves, shares, messages and mentions by the right people.

### Reading website and enquiry numbers

The website is where paid and organic effort turn into enquiries, so the report should include the following.

**Sessions by channel.** Where visitors came from: organic search, paid search, paid social, direct, referral and so on. Check the channel labels make sense. A large "direct" or "unassigned" share often means tracking tags are missing, which is why [UTM tracking and campaign naming](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-utm-tracking-campaign-naming-2026/) is worth agreeing at the start.

**Enquiry rate.** Enquiries divided by sessions, per channel. It tells you whether a channel brings the right people and whether the website does its job. A channel with many visits and almost no enquiries is a prompt to examine the landing page, the audience or the offer.

**Form, call and WhatsApp counts, reconciled with reality.** The numbers in the report should be checkable against your own inbox, call log and WhatsApp inbox. If analytics says forty form submissions and you received twenty-five, find out why. Duplicate submissions, test entries, spam and double-counted events are common.

**Spam and junk.** Spam submissions are counted as leads in many setups. Ask whether the report excludes them. Our guide on [contact form spam and bot protection](/blog/website-designer-pune-contact-form-spam-bot-protection-2026/) explains how it creeps in.

### The most important column: lead quality

A report that counts enquiries but not their quality will push an agency, intentionally or not, towards cheap and plentiful leads rather than good ones. The fix is to close the loop with your own sales data.

Create a simple shared sheet where your team marks each enquiry: genuine or not, qualified or not, and whether it became a sale. Ask the agency to include those columns in their report, by channel and campaign. Then the useful figure appears: cost per qualified enquiry and cost per sale, not cost per click.

For some advertisers, it is possible to send those outcomes back to the ad platform so its algorithms learn what a good lead looks like. Our guides on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026/) and [Meta Conversions API lead tracking](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-meta-conversions-api-lead-tracking-2026/) explain how, and what to be careful about.

### Questions to ask when a number looks too good (or too bad)

A good report invites questions. These are fair to ask any agency.

- **"Where does this number come from?"** The platform, analytics, Search Console, or the agency's own tracking? Different tools disagree, and you should know which is being used.
- **"What is counted as a conversion here?"**
- **"How many of these were genuine enquiries?"**
- **"What was the date range, and is it comparable to last month's?"** A month with a festival or exam season is not comparable to a quiet one.
- **"What changed, and what did you do about it?"**
- **"What will you do differently next month?"**

A good agency answers calmly and shows the data. A weak one becomes defensive or falls back on jargon. How the conversation goes is information.

### Common ways reports mislead without lying

Most misleading reports are not fraudulent. They flatter in predictable ways.

**Cherry-picked date ranges.** A chart that starts at a low point makes growth look dramatic. Ask for the same period year on year where data exists.

**Percentages from tiny bases.** "Enquiries up 200%" can mean two became six. Always see the absolute numbers.

**Averages that hide the spread.** One strong campaign can mask three that waste money. Ask for results per campaign.

**Attribution that credits the last touch.** If someone sees an ad, then later searches your name and enquires, the brand search may get the credit. Ask how attribution is handled and accept that no model is perfect.

**Self-attributed results.** Platforms like to credit themselves. Google and Meta can both claim the same sale. Your own records are the check.

**Vanity metrics front and centre.** Follower counts, impressions and video views are easy to show and easy to grow. Their prominence is a hint.

### Keeping your own record

Do not rely only on the agency's report. A small record of your own protects you and improves the conversation.

- **Own the accounts.** Your Google Ads, Meta, Search Console and analytics accounts should be in your name, with the agency as a user. Our [onboarding checklist](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-onboarding-access-tracking-checklist-2026/) covers this.
- **Know the data limits.** Analytics tools keep some data for a limited time. Google's help page on [data retention](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7667196) explains that GA4 lets you choose how long it keeps certain user-level data, and that the maximum is limited, so if you want a long record you should export it. Search Console keeps a limited history too, so export it periodically.
- **Keep a monthly one-pager.** Spend, enquiries, genuine enquiries, qualified enquiries, sales, cost per genuine enquiry and cost per sale, by channel. You can fill it from the agency's data and your own, and then compare.

### A one-page report you can ask for

Here is a layout you can hand to any agency. It is deliberately short.

**Section 1: The month in numbers.** Total spend (ad spend plus fees), total enquiries, genuine enquiries, qualified enquiries, sales or bookings and the cost per genuine enquiry and per sale. Show last month and the same month last year if available.

**Section 2: By channel.** The same figures split into paid search, paid social, organic search, social, WhatsApp and referral.

**Section 3: What we did.** A short list of the work completed: campaigns launched or paused, pages changed, content published, tests run.

**Section 4: What we learned.** Two or three honest observations, including what did not work.

**Section 5: What we will do next month and why.** Specific actions with the reason for each.

**Section 6: What we need from you.** Approvals, content, access, or sales feedback on lead quality.

Everything else is an appendix. If the agency wants to include impressions and followers, they can go there.

### Worked example: two reports for the same month

Consider a hypothetical Pune dental clinic. This is an illustration; the numbers are invented to show the method and are not benchmarks.

Report A opens with total impressions, a rise in followers and a chart of website visits. Page three mentions "42 conversions". Nothing in it says what a conversion is.

When the clinic's manager asks, it turns out the account counts every click on the phone number, including repeat taps by the same person, and every visit to the contact page as a conversion. Checking the clinic's own phone log and appointment book, there were far fewer real enquiries and fewer bookings.

Report B opens with spend, enquiries received by form, call and WhatsApp, the number the front desk marked as genuine and the number that booked an appointment. It then shows cost per booking by campaign. One campaign is clearly weaker and is paused, with the budget moved to another.

The clinic does not need Report B to be flattering. It needs it to be checkable. The second report lets the owner decide, the first does not.

### What a good agency report feels like

You should come away able to answer, in your own words, what you spent, what you got and what happens next. You should have been shown something that did not work and what was done about it. You should be able to check the key figures against your own records. And you should feel invited to question it.

If you are at the stage of choosing an agency, our guide to [pricing for SEO services](/blog/seo-agency-pricing-india-2026/) explains how to compare proposals, and ask for a sample report before signing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What should a monthly digital marketing report include?

It should show total spend, enquiries received, how many were genuine and qualified, sales or bookings, and the cost per genuine enquiry and per sale, split by channel. It should also list the work done, what was learned and what comes next. Impressions and followers belong in an appendix.

### Which digital marketing metrics actually matter?

Those closest to revenue: qualified enquiries, sales or bookings, and the cost of each. Clicks, visits and engagement help diagnose problems, and impressions and followers are context. The further a metric is from money, the less weight it should carry.

### Why do my agency's numbers not match my own enquiry count?

Different sources count differently. Analytics may include duplicates, spam or weak actions such as page visits, and ad platforms may claim the same result. Reconcile the report against your own inbox, call log and booking records, and ask the agency what counts as a conversion.

### How often should I review a marketing report?

Monthly is sensible for most small businesses, with a brief check of spend and enquiries weekly during active campaigns. Judge results over several months rather than days, particularly for SEO.

### Should I own my ad and analytics accounts?

Yes. Accounts held in your own name, with the agency as a user, let you verify spend and data, and keep your history if you change agency. Be cautious of any arrangement where you cannot log in to your own accounts.

## Where to Start

Ask your agency for last month's report in the one-page format above. Fill in the genuine enquiry and sales columns from your own records, then compare. Do not worry if the first version is rough: the aim is a shared definition of success.
